title: How to salvage fraternities: Challenging young men to be virtuous is better than telling them to avoid being bad
author: Anthony B. Bradley
summary: In this Boston Globe op-ed, Acton Institute research fellow Anthony Bradley argues that the response to fraternity scandals such as the alleged Cornell assault should be a vision of heroic character rather than only punitive sanctions or abolition. He began a book on fraternity vice in 2021 but was redirected after meeting members at UVA's Sigma Phi, finding that fraternity men want to be good men but do not know how, and so improvise rites of passage around sexual conquest, substance abuse, athletics and professional success. He contends that college presidents and national fraternities should instead tell pledges to define their presence on campus by virtue, and cites Clemson's Chi Psi "Gentlemen's Club" and Lambda Chi Alpha's "Ideal Man Code" as working examples. He notes that young men arrive with self-doubt, loneliness, anxiety and addiction and that about 250,000 undergraduates belong to fraternities, a ready channel for formation. His closing claim is that raising the bar is more effective than asking men to be less bad than other chapters.
points: Fraternity men want to be good, but lacking guidance they invent rites of passage built on conquest, substance abuse, athletics and career success.
Bradley argues that inviting men to heroic character (safest houses for women, caring for campus, mentoring pledges) works better than merely prohibiting hazing and assault.
Concrete models exist: a weekly Gentlemen's Club at Clemson's Chi Psi and Lambda Chi Alpha's Ideal Man Code that recenters the culture on character formation.
Universities are urged to partner with national fraternities on character formation rather than relying on sanctions alone.
The op-ed treats fraternities as an underused channel for forming young men who arrive with loneliness, anxiety and performance pressure.
quotes: Fraternity men categorically want to be good men, but they do not know how. They want to contribute positively to campus life and to society, but they have no direction on what that looks like in practice.
In the absence of guidance, they make up their own rites of passage — namely, sexual conquest, substance abuse, athletic performance, and professional success.
Enlist fraternity men to be men of heroic character and give them an aspirational vision for what that looks like on campus.
At least since the movie “Animal House,” college men have followed a rite-of-passage script centered on vice, not virtue.

Indeed, young men today are arriving on campus with profound challenges. Many are full of self-doubt, struggling with anxiety and depression, loneliness, performance pressure, addiction, and disordered definitions of fun.
Telling men that their school expects them to be great — and holding them to that standard — would be more effective than asking them to be less bad than their counterparts in other chapters.
Merely telling men not to haze or to avoid committing sexual assault is not inviting men to excellence. If we raise the bar, they will aspire to it.
